claim: Plexins exhibit multitudinous, evolutionarily conserved functions in neural development.
source: Plexins exhibit multitudinous, evolutionarily conserved functions in neural development.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature on Plexins.

claim: PlexB controls multiple steps during the assembly of the Drosophila olfactory circuit.
source: We previously reported that Plexin B (PlexB) controls multiple steps during the assembly of the Drosophila olfactory circuit (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The extracellular Sema domain is essential for axon fasciculation, trajectory choice, and synaptic partner selection.
source: We found that the extracellular Sema domain is essential for all three steps
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2C, 3C, and 4C showing that deletion of the Sema domain abolishes PlexB function in all three processes.

claim: The catalytic site of the intracellular RapGAP is not engaged in axon fasciculation, trajectory choice, or synaptic partner selection.
source: the catalytic site of the intracellular RapGAP is engaged in none
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2D, 3D, and 4D showing that the GAPmut variant rescues or functions similarly to wild-type PlexB.

claim: The intracellular GTPase-binding motifs are essential for trajectory choice and synaptic partner selection.
source: the intracellular GTPase-binding motifs are essential for trajectory choice and synaptic partner selection
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 3E-G and 4E-G showing that disruption of GTPase-binding sites impairs these functions.

claim: The intracellular GTPase-binding motifs are dispensable for fasciculation.
source: the intracellular GTPase-binding motifs are essential for trajectory choice and synaptic partner selection, but are dispensable for fasciculation
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2E-G showing that GTPase-binding mutants can rescue fasciculation defects.

claim: Extracellular PlexB cleavage serves as a regulatory mechanism of PlexB signaling.
source: Moreover, extracellular PlexB cleavage serves as a regulatory mechanism of PlexB signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that uncleavable PlexB has enhanced activity (Figures 2H, 3H) and that cleaved fragments can reconstitute function (Figure 3K).

claim: The divergent roles of PlexB motifs in distinct steps of neural development contribute to its functional versatility in neural circuit assembly.
source: Thus, the divergent roles of PlexB motifs in distinct steps of neural development contribute to its functional versatility in neural circuit assembly.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential motif requirements across developmental processes.

claim: Plexin-family receptors are over 600 million years old.
source: Over 600 million years old, Plexin-family receptors display high degrees of conservation across evolutionarily distant species for both extracellular and cytoplasmic domains (Junqueira Alves et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work on Plexin evolution.

claim: Plexin-family receptors display high degrees of conservation across evolutionarily distant species for both extracellular and cytoplasmic domains.
source: Over 600 million years old, Plexin-family receptors display high degrees of conservation across evolutionarily distant species for both extracellular and cytoplasmic domains (Junqueira Alves et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work on Plexin conservation.

claim: The extracellular Sema domain is a core domain required for Plexin signaling.
source: Structural and biochemical investigations have identified several core domains required for Plexin signaling (Bell et al., 2011; He et al., 2009; Janssen et al., 2010; Janssen et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010; Shang et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2007; Tong et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013): the extracellular Sema domain
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The intracellular Rac and Rho GTPase-binding sites are core domains required for Plexin signaling.
source: Structural and biochemical investigations have identified several core domains required for Plexin signaling (Bell et al., 2011; He et al., 2009; Janssen et al., 2010; Janssen et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010; Shang et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2007; Tong et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013): the extracellular Sema domain, the intracellular Rac and Rho GTPase-binding sites
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The intracellular catalytic RapGAP domain is a core domain required for Plexin signaling.
source: Structural and biochemical investigations have identified several core domains required for Plexin signaling (Bell et al., 2011; He et al., 2009; Janssen et al., 2010; Janssen et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010; Shang et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2007; Tong et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013): the extracellular Sema domain, the intracellular Rac and Rho GTPase-binding sites, and the intracellular catalytic RapGAP domain
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies, though the authors' data suggests it may not be universally required.

claim: Concomitant Semaphorin extracellular binding and Rac intracellular binding lead to Plexin dimerization.
source: the current working model of Plexin signal transduction suggests that concomitant Semaphorin extracellular binding and Rac intracellular binding lead to Plexin dimerization
evidence: This is a description of the current working model in the field, supported by citation to a review.

claim: Plexin dimerization activates the catalytic GAP domain to hydrolyze Rap-GTP for downstream signaling.
source: the current working model of Plexin signal transduction suggests that concomitant Semaphorin extracellular binding and Rac intracellular binding lead to Plexin dimerization, which subsequently activates the catalytic GAP domain to hydrolyze Rap-GTP for downstream signaling (Pascoe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the current working model in the field, supported by citation to a review.

claim: The catalytic GAP domain is essential in neural tube closure.
source: Notably, the catalytic GAP domain has been shown to be essential in neural tube closure (Worzfeld et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The catalytic GAP domain is not essential in motor axon guidance.
source: Notably, the catalytic GAP domain has been shown to be essential in neural tube closure (Worzfeld et al., 2014) but not in motor axon guidance (Yang et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Plexins may use structural motifs differentially in distinct developmental contexts.
source: suggesting that Plexins may use structural motifs differentially in distinct developmental contexts
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential requirement of the GAP domain in different processes.

claim: The convertase cleavage site is a conserved signature of all class B Plexins.
source: We particularly note the convertase cleavage site – a conserved signature of all class B Plexins (Artigiani et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: No biological function of the convertase cleavage site has been reported since its discovery over a decade ago.
source: Despite its conservation across hundreds of millions of years, to our knowledge no biological function has ever been reported since its discovery over a decade ago.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: The cleavage event physically separates the extracellular and transmembrane-cytoplasmic parts of Plexin.
source: Considering that the cleavage event breaks the Plexin protein and thus physically separates the extracellular and transmembrane-cytoplasmic parts
evidence: This is a logical inference from the nature of protein cleavage.

claim: PlexB plays indispensable roles in multiple steps during the assembly of the Drosophila olfactory map.
source: We recently reported that PlexB plays indispensable roles in multiple steps during the assembly of the Drosophila olfactory map, with level-independent functions in the axon fasciculation of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and level-dependent tasks in ORN axon trajectory choice and subsequent glomerular targeting (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: PlexB has level-independent functions in the axon fasciculation of olfactory receptor neurons.
source: We recently reported that PlexB plays indispensable roles in multiple steps during the assembly of the Drosophila olfactory map, with level-independent functions in the axon fasciculation of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and level-dependent tasks in ORN axon trajectory choice and subsequent glomerular targeting (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: PlexB has level-dependent tasks in ORN axon trajectory choice.
source: We recently reported that PlexB plays indispensable roles in multiple steps during the assembly of the Drosophila olfactory map, with level-independent functions in the axon fasciculation of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and level-dependent tasks in ORN axon trajectory choice and subsequent glomerular targeting (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: PlexB has level-dependent tasks in glomerular targeting.
source: We recently reported that PlexB plays indispensable roles in multiple steps during the assembly of the Drosophila olfactory map, with level-independent functions in the axon fasciculation of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and level-dependent tasks in ORN axon trajectory choice and subsequent glomerular targeting (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: PlexB regulates axon-axon interaction (fasciculation) in the Drosophila olfactory system.
source: These findings reveal that, within one system, PlexB regulates several fundamental cellular processes of neural wiring, namely axon-axon interaction (fasciculation), axon guidance (trajectory choice), and synaptic partner selection (glomerular targeting) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and data presented in the current study.

claim: PlexB regulates axon guidance (trajectory choice) in the Drosophila olfactory system.
source: These findings reveal that, within one system, PlexB regulates several fundamental cellular processes of neural wiring, namely axon-axon interaction (fasciculation), axon guidance (trajectory choice), and synaptic partner selection (glomerular targeting) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and data presented in the current study.

claim: PlexB regulates synaptic partner selection (glomerular targeting) in the Drosophila olfactory system.
source: These findings reveal that, within one system, PlexB regulates several fundamental cellular processes of neural wiring, namely axon-axon interaction (fasciculation), axon guidance (trajectory choice), and synaptic partner selection (glomerular targeting) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and data presented in the current study.

claim: PlexB likely signals in different ways when executing distinct developmental tasks.
source: Given that this level dependence is only observed in trajectory choice and glomerular targeting but not in fasciculation, it is likely that PlexB signals in different ways when executing these distinct tasks.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential level-dependence of PlexB functions.

claim: Nine UAS transgenic lines carrying PlexB variants were generated.
source: To dissect the structure-to-function relationship of PlexB in the assembly of the fly olfactory map, we generated nine UAS transgenic lines carrying PlexB variants (described below; Figure 1B) produced by site-directed mutagenesis.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: A V5 tag was added to the C-terminus of each PlexB variant.
source: A V5 tag was added to the C-terminus of each variant.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: All PlexB transgenes were integrated into the same genomic locus, ZH-attP-86Fb.
source: To obtain comparable expression levels, all transgenes were mutagenized from a single wild-type UAS-PlexB construct (Joo et al., 2013) and integrated into the same genomic locus, ZH-attP-86Fb (Bischof et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Expression of PlexB variants in Drosophila neurons in vivo was verified by Western blotting with an anti-V5 antibody.
source: Their expression in Drosophila neurons in vivo was verified by Western blotting with an anti-V5 antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extracellular Sema domain mediates binding between Plexins and Semaphorins.
source: It mediates binding between Plexins and Semaphorins and triggers Plexin signal transduction (Janssen et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: The Sema domain triggers Plexin signal transduction.
source: It mediates binding between Plexins and Semaphorins and triggers Plexin signal transduction (Janssen et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: PlexB with its entire Sema domain deleted (∆Sema) was expressed and cleaved normally in vivo.
source: PlexB with its entire Sema domain deleted (∆Sema) was expressed and cleaved normally in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Ras homolog Rap is the substrate of the Plexin GAP domain for signal transduction.
source: Recent studies identified the Ras homolog Rap as its substrate for signal transduction (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Three arginine residues are essential for the GAP catalytic activity in fly PlexB.
source: With homology alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we identified the three arginine residues that are essential for the GAP catalytic activity (Wang et al., 2012; Worzfeld et al., 2014) in fly PlexB
evidence: This claim is supported by homology alignment data and citations to published studies.

claim: The GAPmut variant (R1570A, R1571G, R1899A) did not affect PlexB's expression and cleavage in vivo.
source: These point mutations did not affect PlexB's expression and cleavage in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GTPase-binding region of fly PlexB interacts with small GTPases Rac1 and Rho1.
source: Sitting between the two arms of the RapGAP domain, the GTPase-binding region of fly PlexB has been shown to interact with small GTPases Rac1 and Rho1 (Hu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Class B Plexins can interact simultaneously with two Rac1 molecules.
source: Structural analysis found that class B Plexins can interact simultaneously with two Rac1 molecules, with one bound at each site (Bell et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published structural study.

claim: Disrupting Rac1 or Rho1 binding reduced the presence of cleaved fragments in brains.
source: Intriguingly, while full-length PlexB proteins were present normally, the cleaved C-terminal fragment was markedly reduced in ∆Rac1 or ∆Rho1 variants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as previously observed in cell culture (Artigiani et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to a previous study.

claim: Only a small fraction of endogenous PlexB proteins are present in the full-length form in developing fly brains.
source: In developing fly brains, only a small fraction of endogenous PlexB proteins are present in the full-length form (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The cleaved C-terminal fragment of PlexB is not degraded in vivo.
source: Notably, the cleaved C-terminal fragment is not degraded in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing stable cleaved fragments.

claim: Cleaved PlexB products stably associate in a complex in cell culture.
source: This is consistent with a previous observation that cleaved PlexB products stably associate in a complex in cell culture (Artigiani et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The two arginine mutations (R1196A, R1199A) abolished PlexB cleavage and increased the presence of full-length PlexB.
source: Indeed, the two arginine mutations abolished PlexB cleavage and increased the presence of full-length PlexB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cleaved fragments, when individually expressed, were stable in vivo.
source: The cleaved fragments, when individually expressed, were also stable in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At about 18 hours after puparium formation (hAPF), ORN axons arrive at the antennal lobe and fasciculate with neighboring axons, forming two discrete bundles.
source: At about 18 hours after puparium formation (hAPF), ORN axons arrive at the antennal lobe and fasciculate with neighboring axons, forming two discrete bundles.
evidence: This is a description of the developmental process based on established knowledge of the system.

claim: Over 6 hours after arrival, ORN axon bundles circumnavigate the antennal lobe.
source: Over the next 6 hr, these two axon bundles circumnavigate the antennal lobe (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: This is a description of the developmental process supported by imaging data.

claim: ORN axon fasciculation is mediated by PlexB-dependent axon-axon interactions.
source: Previously, we found that ORN axon fasciculation is mediated by PlexB-dependent axon-axon interactions (Joo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: In PlexB loss-of-function mutants (plexB–/–), ORN axon defasciculation was observed in almost every antennal lobe with differing severity.
source: In PlexB loss-of-function mutants (plexB–/–), ORN axon defasciculation was observed in almost every antennal lobe with differing severity (Figure 2A, middle and right panels; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of a wild-type PlexB transgene in ORNs significantly restored axon fasciculation in plexB–/– flies.
source: In plexB–/– flies, expression of a wild-type PlexB transgene in ORNs significantly restored axon fasciculation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ORN-specific rescue of PlexB was not complete.
source: However, ORN-specific rescue was not complete (Figure 2B), suggesting that PlexB supplied by other cellular sources may also contribute to ORN axon fasciculation.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PlexB supplied by other cellular sources may contribute to ORN axon fasciculation.
source: However, ORN-specific rescue was not complete (Figure 2B), suggesting that PlexB supplied by other cellular sources may also contribute to ORN axon fasciculation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the incomplete rescue observed in the data.

claim: The rescue by Sema domain-deleted PlexB completely failed in fasciculation.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, the rescue by Sema domain-deleted PlexB completely failed, indicating the necessity of the Sema domain in PlexB-mediated fasciculation.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Sema domain is necessary for PlexB-mediated fasciculation.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, the rescue by Sema domain-deleted PlexB completely failed, indicating the necessity of the Sema domain in PlexB-mediated fasciculation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: None of the intracellular motifs assayed were required for fasciculation.
source: On the other hand, none of the intracellular motifs we assayed were required, as none of the mutants displayed a compromised ability to rescue fasciculation defects (Figure 2D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 2D-G.

claim: Either the cytoplasmic signaling is not required for fasciculation, or different motifs play redundant roles in mediating fasciculation.
source: These data suggest that either the cytoplasmic signaling is not required for fasciculation, or that different motifs play redundant roles in mediating fasciculation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data regarding the role of cytoplasmic motifs.

claim: Uncleavable PlexB exhibited better rescue than wild-type PlexB in fasciculation.
source: Notably, uncleavable PlexB appeared to exhibit better rescue than wild-type PlexB, with only one severe defasciculation case out of 47 examined (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Full-length PlexB proteins play a predominant role in mediating axon fasciculation.
source: Considering that uncleavable PlexB only supplies full-length PlexB proteins, this finding suggests that the full-length PlexB proteins play a predominant role in mediating axon fasciculation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enhanced activity of uncleavable PlexB.

claim: Neither the N- nor C- terminal cleaved products exhibited any rescue effects in fasciculation when expressed separately.
source: Consistently, neither the N- nor C- terminal cleaved products, when expressed separately (Figure 2I,J) or together (Figure 2K), exhibited any rescue effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 2I-K.

claim: The N- and C- terminal cleaved products did not exhibit rescue effects when expressed together in fasciculation.
source: Consistently, neither the N- nor C- terminal cleaved products, when expressed separately (Figure 2I,J) or together (Figure 2K), exhibited any rescue effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: PlexB-dependent axon fasciculation is mediated by full-length PlexB but not the cleaved fragments.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that PlexB-dependent axon fasciculation is mediated by full-length PlexB but not the cleaved fragments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on fasciculation.

claim: Fasciculation does not require any individual cytoplasmic signaling motif but relies on the extracellular Sema domain.
source: Moreover, fasciculation appears to not require any individual cytoplasmic signaling motif but relies on the extracellular Sema domain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on fasciculation.

claim: PlexB-dependent axon fasciculation is likely an intercellular adhesion process.
source: Thus, PlexB-dependent axon fasciculation is likely an intercellular adhesion process, in which full-length PlexB proteins bundle axons together through Sema domain-mediated molecular adhesion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the data based on the requirement for the Sema domain and dispensability of cytoplasmic motifs.

claim: Individual ORN axons choose one of two trajectories – dorsolateral (DL) or ventromedial (VM) – after arrival at the ventrolateral corner of the antennal lobe at around 18hAPF.
source: After their arrival at the ventrolateral corner of the antennal lobe at around 18hAPF, individual ORN axons choose one of the two trajectories – dorsolateral (DL) or ventromedial (VM) – and then circumnavigate the antennal lobe in the next 6 hours (Figure 3A; left panels) (Jefferis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of the developmental process supported by citation and imaging data.

claim: Axons of each ORN class stereotypically choose one defined trajectory.
source: Importantly, axons of each ORN class stereotypically choose one defined trajectory.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the olfactory system.

claim: Trajectory choice is regulated by the axonal PlexB level.
source: We previously found that trajectory choice is regulated by the axonal PlexB level: a high PlexB level drives axons to the DL trajectory while a low PlexB level confers a VM choice (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: A high PlexB level drives axons to the DL trajectory.
source: We previously found that trajectory choice is regulated by the axonal PlexB level: a high PlexB level drives axons to the DL trajectory while a low PlexB level confers a VM choice (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: A low PlexB level confers a VM trajectory choice.
source: We previously found that trajectory choice is regulated by the axonal PlexB level: a high PlexB level drives axons to the DL trajectory while a low PlexB level confers a VM choice (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: PlexB overexpression in ORNs shifts axons to the DL trajectory.
source: Consequently, PlexB overexpression in ORNs shifts axons to the DL trajectory (Figure 3A; right panels) (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 3A and citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type PlexB in ORNs raised the mean DL/VM ratio to 0.94 from 0.67 of controls.
source: Recapitulating our previous observations, overexpression of wild-type PlexB in ORNs drove axons to the DL bundle, raising the mean DL/VM ratio to 0.94 from 0.67 of controls (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sema2a and Sema2b establish a gradient along the VM-to-DL axis between 18–24hAPF to instruct PlexB-expressing ORN axons in trajectory choice.
source: Between 18–24hAPF, the canonical ligands of PlexB—Sema2a and Sema2b—establish a gradient along the VM-to-DL axis to instruct PlexB-expressing ORN axons in trajectory choice (Joo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of the Sema domain completely disrupted the ability of PlexB to drive a DL shift in trajectory choice.
source: In line with this, deletion of the Sema domain that mediates the Plexin-Semaphorin interaction completely disrupted the ability of PlexB to drive a DL shift (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutating either Rac1- or Rho1- binding sites impaired the DL shift caused by PlexB overexpression.
source: Regarding the cytoplasmic motifs, mutating either Rac1- or Rho1- binding sites impaired, at least partially, the DL shift caused by PlexB overexpression (Figure 3E–G), revealing the functional necessity of PlexB-GTPase interactions in trajectory choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 3E-G.

claim: PlexB-GTPase interactions are functionally necessary in trajectory choice.
source: Regarding the cytoplasmic motifs, mutating either Rac1- or Rho1- binding sites impaired, at least partially, the DL shift caused by PlexB overexpression (Figure 3E–G), revealing the functional necessity of PlexB-GTPase interactions in trajectory choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 3E-G.

claim: Deleting the first Rac1-binding site (∆Rac1) entirely abolished the DL shift caused by PlexB overexpression.
source: Notably, while deleting the first of the Rac1-binding sites (∆Rac1) entirely abolished the DL shift caused by PlexB overexpression (Figure 3E)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutating the second Rac1-binding site (Rac1mut) only partially weakened the DL shift phenotype.
source: mutating the second Rac1-binding site (Rac1mut) only partially weakened the phenotype (Figure 3F), suggesting the differential importance of these sites in mediating the PlexB-Rac1 interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The two Rac1-binding sites have differential importance in mediating the PlexB-Rac1 interaction.
source: mutating the second Rac1-binding site (Rac1mut) only partially weakened the phenotype (Figure 3F), suggesting the differential importance of these sites in mediating the PlexB-Rac1 interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of mutating the two Rac1-binding sites.

claim: The catalytic RapGAP domain was not required for trajectory choice.
source: Interestingly, the catalytic RapGAP domain was not required (Figure 3D), as in PlexA-dependent motor axon guidance (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D and comparison to a cited study.

claim: Uncleavable PlexB was significantly more potent than wild-type PlexB at driving DL shift in trajectory choice.
source: We then examined the involvement of PlexB cleavage in trajectory choice and found that uncleavable PlexB was significantly more potent than wild-type PlexB at driving DL shift (Figure 3H), suggesting that full-length PlexB proteins are more active for this function.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Full-length PlexB proteins are more active for trajectory choice.
source: We then examined the involvement of PlexB cleavage in trajectory choice and found that uncleavable PlexB was significantly more potent than wild-type PlexB at driving DL shift (Figure 3H), suggesting that full-length PlexB proteins are more active for this function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enhanced activity of uncleavable PlexB.

claim: The cleavage of PlexB limits the level of full-length PlexB proteins.
source: Considering that trajectory choice is a PlexB level-dependent process (Li et al., 2018b), the cleavage of PlexB thus limits the level of full-length PlexB proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and can potentially regulate the fidelity of trajectory choice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the level-dependence of trajectory choice and the effect of cleavage on full-length protein levels.

claim: PlexB cleavage can potentially regulate the fidelity of trajectory choice.
source: Considering that trajectory choice is a PlexB level-dependent process (Li et al., 2018b), the cleavage of PlexB thus limits the level of full-length PlexB proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and can potentially regulate the fidelity of trajectory choice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the regulatory role of cleavage.

claim: The cleaved fragments did not show any function individually in trajectory choice.
source: Intriguingly, while the cleaved fragments did not show any function individually (Figure 3I,J), simultaneous expression of both partially but significantly promoted DL shift of ORN axons (Figure 3K)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 3I and 3J.

claim: Simultaneous expression of both cleaved fragments partially but significantly promoted DL shift of ORN axons in trajectory choice.
source: Intriguingly, while the cleaved fragments did not show any function individually (Figure 3I,J), simultaneous expression of both partially but significantly promoted DL shift of ORN axons (Figure 3K), indicating the functional reconstitution of cleaved fragments in vivo for signaling in trajectory choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Cleaved fragments can functionally reconstitute in vivo for signaling in trajectory choice.
source: Intriguingly, while the cleaved fragments did not show any function individually (Figure 3I,J), simultaneous expression of both partially but significantly promoted DL shift of ORN axons (Figure 3K), indicating the functional reconstitution of cleaved fragments in vivo for signaling in trajectory choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that co-expression of both fragments has activity.

claim: PlexB instructs axon trajectory choice by engaging both extracellular and cytoplasmic components.
source: In summary, distinct from its adhesion-like function in axon fasciculation (Figure 2), PlexB instructs axon trajectory choice by engaging both extracellular and cytoplasmic components, although the RapGAP catalytic activity appears dispensable.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on trajectory choice.

claim: The RapGAP catalytic activity appears dispensable for trajectory choice.
source: In summary, distinct from its adhesion-like function in axon fasciculation (Figure 2), PlexB instructs axon trajectory choice by engaging both extracellular and cytoplasmic components, although the RapGAP catalytic activity appears dispensable.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that GAPmut can function in trajectory choice.

claim: Cleavage of PlexB can regulate the strength of PlexB signaling in trajectory choice.
source: Cleavage of PlexB can regulate the strength of PlexB signaling, as the full-length protein appeared to be more active, while the reconstituted fragments also exhibited activity in trajectory choice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on the effects of cleavage.

claim: Between 24–48hAPF, ORN axons innervate the antennal lobe and search for the dendrites of their synaptic partners—olfactory projection neurons (PNs).
source: Between 24–48hAPF, ORN axons innervate the antennal lobe and search for the dendrites of their synaptic partners—olfactory projection neurons (PNs).
evidence: This is a description of the developmental process based on established knowledge.

claim: By 48hAPF, the antennal lobe has been divided into roughly 50 proto-glomeruli.
source: By 48hAPF, the antennal lobe has been divided into roughly 50 proto-glomeruli, where the axons and dendrites of matching ORNs and PNs interact (Jefferis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of the developmental process supported by citation.

claim: PlexB plays a level-dependent role in instructing glomerular selection of ORN axons, independently of trajectory choice.
source: We previously found that PlexB plays a level-dependent role in instructing glomerular selection of ORN axons, independently of trajectory choice (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: ORN axons targeting to several discrete glomeruli express higher levels of PlexB than their neighbors.
source: Specifically, ORN axons targeting to several discrete glomeruli express higher levels of PlexB than their neighbors.
evidence: This is a description of the expression pattern based on previous work.

claim: PlexB-high glomeruli localize mainly in the medial antennal lobe, such as DM1 and DM5, along with a few scattered glomeruli, like VA4.
source: These PlexB-high glomeruli localize mainly in the medial antennal lobe, such as DM1 and DM5, along with a few scattered glomeruli, like VA4.
evidence: This is a description of the spatial distribution of PlexB-high glomeruli based on previous work.

claim: PlexB overexpression in ORNs promotes mistargeting of ORN axons to PlexB-high glomeruli.
source: PlexB overexpression in ORNs promotes mistargeting of ORN axons to PlexB-high glomeruli, while RNAi-based knockdown shows the opposite preference (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: RNAi-based knockdown of PlexB shows the opposite preference to overexpression in glomerular targeting.
source: PlexB overexpression in ORNs promotes mistargeting of ORN axons to PlexB-high glomeruli, while RNAi-based knockdown shows the opposite preference (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: PlexB overexpression caused mistargeting of VA2 ORN axons stereotypically to the DM5 glomerulus.
source: In line with our previous observations, PlexB overexpression caused mistargeting of VA2 ORN axons stereotypically to the DM5 glomerulus (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: PlexB without its Sema domain failed to induce glomerular mistargeting.
source: PlexB without its Sema domain failed to induce glomerular mistargeting (Figure 4C), emphasizing the global necessity of Sema domain in all wiring processes examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Sema domain is globally necessary in all wiring processes examined.
source: PlexB without its Sema domain failed to induce glomerular mistargeting (Figure 4C), emphasizing the global necessity of Sema domain in all wiring processes examined.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the requirement of the Sema domain in all three processes tested.

claim: The RapGAP catalytic site was not essential for synaptic partner selection.
source: In contrast, the RapGAP catalytic site was not essential for any tested processes, including synaptic partner selection (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Glomerular targeting required PlexB-GTPase interactions.
source: As in trajectory choice, glomerular targeting required PlexB-GTPase interactions, as the variants disrupting Rac1- or Rho1- binding sites substantially reduced glomerular mistargeting events caused by PlexB overexpression (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 4E-G.

claim: Variants disrupting Rac1- or Rho1- binding sites substantially reduced glomerular mistargeting events caused by PlexB overexpression.
source: As in trajectory choice, glomerular targeting required PlexB-GTPase interactions, as the variants disrupting Rac1- or Rho1- binding sites substantially reduced glomerular mistargeting events caused by PlexB overexpression (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 4E-G.

claim: Deletion of the first Rac1-binding site resulted in greater functional disruption than substitution at the second site in glomerular targeting.
source: Notably, deletion of the first Rac1-binding site again resulted in greater functional disruption than substitution at the second site (Figure 4E,F; as well as Figure 3E,F), further supporting the differential importance of these two regions in bridging PlexB and Rac1.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: The two Rac1-binding regions have differential importance in bridging PlexB and Rac1.
source: Notably, deletion of the first Rac1-binding site again resulted in greater functional disruption than substitution at the second site (Figure 4E,F; as well as Figure 3E,F), further supporting the differential importance of these two regions in bridging PlexB and Rac1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects observed across multiple assays.

claim: Overexpression of the cleaved products, either independently or together, was insufficient to drive mistargeting in synaptic partner selection.
source: Overexpression of the cleaved products, either independently or together, was insufficient to drive mistargeting (Figure 4I–K), suggesting that synaptic partner selection is likely mediated by the full-length PlexB.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 4I-K.

claim: Synaptic partner selection is likely mediated by the full-length PlexB.
source: Overexpression of the cleaved products, either independently or together, was insufficient to drive mistargeting (Figure 4I–K), suggesting that synaptic partner selection is likely mediated by the full-length PlexB.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of activity of cleaved fragments in this assay.

claim: Uncleavable PlexB did not increase the phenotypic penetrance in synaptic partner selection compared to wild-type.
source: However, uncleavable PlexB, which produces more full-length proteins than wild-type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), did not increase the phenotypic penetrance (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: PlexB-mediated synaptic partner selection engages both extracellular and cytoplasmic modules for signaling.
source: Collectively, PlexB-mediated synaptic partner selection engages both extracellular and cytoplasmic modules for signaling, resembling trajectory choice but not axon fasciculation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on synaptic partner selection.

claim: PlexB-mediated synaptic partner selection resembles trajectory choice but not axon fasciculation in terms of motif engagement.
source: Collectively, PlexB-mediated synaptic partner selection engages both extracellular and cytoplasmic modules for signaling, resembling trajectory choice but not axon fasciculation.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion drawn from the patterns of motif requirements across the three processes.

claim: Extracellular cleavage of PlexB does not appear to be critical in synaptic partner selection.
source: Moreover, extracellular cleavage of PlexB does not appear to be critical in synaptic partner selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of enhanced activity of uncleavable PlexB in this assay.

claim: PlexB achieves functional versatility in neurodevelopment by diversified and task-specific motif engagement.
source: These experiments reveal how a single molecule, PlexB, achieves functional versatility in neurodevelopment by diversified and task-specific motif engagement, in conjunction with temporally-regulated expression and level-dependent signaling as we previously discovered (Li et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating the current findings with previous work.

claim: The systematic in vivo analysis shows the divergent engagement of different PlexB structural motifs in distinct neurodevelopmental processes.
source: Our systematic in vivo analysis shows the divergent engagement of different PlexB structural motifs in distinct neurodevelopmental processes (Figure 5), arguing against a singular signaling mechanism for PlexB.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis presented in the study.

claim: The findings argue against a singular signaling mechanism for PlexB.
source: Our systematic in vivo analysis shows the divergent engagement of different PlexB structural motifs in distinct neurodevelopmental processes (Figure 5), arguing against a singular signaling mechanism for PlexB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of differential motif requirements.

claim: Cleavage is a regulatory mechanism of PlexB signaling in vivo.
source: We further identify cleavage as a regulatory mechanism of PlexB signaling in vivo, highlighting the functional significance of the evolutionarily conserved cleavage of class B Plexins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on cleavage effects.

claim: The evolutionarily conserved cleavage of class B Plexins has functional significance.
source: We further identify cleavage as a regulatory mechanism of PlexB signaling in vivo, highlighting the functional significance of the evolutionarily conserved cleavage of class B Plexins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the demonstration of cleavage's regulatory role.

claim: In vivo studies in different developmental systems have yielded contrasting observations regarding the functional significance of the RapGAP catalytic activity.
source: Although structural and in vitro studies have pinned down Rap as the substrate for Plexin's GAP domains (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013), in vivo studies in different developmental systems have yielded contrasting observations regarding the functional significance of its catalytic activity (Worzfeld et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing different requirements for GAP activity.

claim: RapGAP-mediated catalysis provides one, but not the only, signaling output of Plexins.
source: Thus, RapGAP-mediated catalysis provides one, but not the only, signaling output of Plexins, further supporting the notion that Plexins diversely engage signaling motifs for distinct developmental tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that GAP activity is not universally required.

claim: Plexins diversely engage signaling motifs for distinct developmental tasks.
source: Thus, RapGAP-mediated catalysis provides one, but not the only, signaling output of Plexins, further supporting the notion that Plexins diversely engage signaling motifs for distinct developmental tasks.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the differential motif requirements observed.

claim: The catalytic arginine residues are conserved and are individually indispensable across species and across Plexin sub-families.
source: Although the catalytic arginine residues are conserved and are individually indispensable across species and across Plexin sub-families (Oinuma et al., 2004; Rohm et al., 2000; Saito et al., 2009; Sakurai et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The integrity of GTPase-binding sites is crucial for PlexB-mediated axon guidance of embryonic motor neurons.
source: It has been shown that the integrity of GTPase-binding sites is crucial for PlexB-mediated axon guidance of embryonic motor neurons (Hu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The GTPase-binding sites are entirely dispensable for bundling ORN axons.
source: While the GTPase-binding sites are entirely dispensable for bundling ORN axons, both axon trajectory choice and synaptic partner selection require proper GTPase binding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on fasciculation.

claim: Both axon trajectory choice and synaptic partner selection require proper GTPase binding.
source: While the GTPase-binding sites are entirely dispensable for bundling ORN axons, both axon trajectory choice and synaptic partner selection require proper GTPase binding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on trajectory choice and synaptic partner selection.

claim: The two distinct Rac1-binding sites are of different importance in mediating the PlexB-Rac1 interaction.
source: Notably, the two distinct Rac1-binding sites are of different importance in mediating the PlexB-Rac1 interaction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the differential effects of mutating the two sites.

claim: Disrupting GTPase binding may cause secondary defects by reducing cleaved PlexB.
source: Disrupting GTPase binding may thus cause secondary defects by reducing cleaved PlexB.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that GTPase-binding mutants have reduced cleaved fragments.

claim: Losing GTPase binding destabilizes the C-terminal cleaved fragment.
source: Rather, it is more likely that losing GTPase binding destabilizes the C-terminal cleaved fragment, which contains a short, degradation-prone extracellular motif.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that GTPase-binding mutants have reduced cleaved fragments.

claim: The cleaved fragments are capable of signaling.
source: Considering that the cleaved fragments are capable of signaling, the interaction between GTPase binding and cleavage adds another layer of complexity to PlexB signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that co-expressed fragments can reconstitute activity.

claim: The interaction between GTPase binding and cleavage adds another layer of complexity to PlexB signaling.
source: Considering that the cleaved fragments are capable of signaling, the interaction between GTPase binding and cleavage adds another layer of complexity to PlexB signaling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that GTPase binding affects cleavage and both affect signaling.

claim: Cleavage brings new properties and regulatory potentials to PlexB.
source: Taken together, cleavage brings new properties and regulatory potentials to PlexB.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the various effects of cleavage observed.
